subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: The first law of thermodynamics and its sign convention
Work done when a gas changes volume
Change in internal energy from change in temperature
Entropy as a measure of disorder
The second law in three forms
The adiabatic equation for a monatomic ideal gas

questions.q: The first law of thermodynamics, Q = ΔU + W, is applied to a closed system using Clausius' sign convention. Which statement about the law is correct?
options: It applies to a system that no energy can enter or leave, because a closed system is sealed off from its surroundings.
Q is the thermal energy that the system contains, and it forms one part of the system's total internal energy U.
Q and W are properties of the state of the system, as U is, so each depends only on the initial and final states.
It is conservation of energy: the thermal energy supplied equals the rise in internal energy plus the work done by the system.
optionWhy: A student who reads 'closed' in its everyday sense picks this. A closed system exchanges no MASS with its surroundings, but energy can cross its boundary as heat and as work; a system that exchanges neither mass nor energy is isolated, and for it Q = W = 0.

A student who thinks of heat as something a body stores picks this. Q is energy transferred because of a temperature difference during a process; what the system contains is internal energy U, and the energy supplied as heat can leave again as work.

A student who treats heat and work as properties of the state picks this. Only U is a property of the state: two different processes between the same states have the same ΔU but can involve different amounts of heat and work.

Energy can cross the boundary of a closed system only as heat or as work. Conservation of energy then requires the thermal energy supplied, Q, to equal the increase in internal energy, ΔU, plus the energy that leaves as work done by the system, W.
questions.explain: Energy can cross the boundary of a closed system only as heat or as work. Conservation of energy then requires the thermal energy supplied, Q, to equal the increase in internal energy, ΔU, plus the energy that leaves as work done by the system, W.

questions.q: Helium, a monatomic ideal gas, is kept at a constant pressure of 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa while it expands from 2.0 dm³ to 5.0 dm³. What is the work W, as it appears in Q = ΔU + W, for this process?
optionWhy: A student who treats W as the work done ON the gas gives the expansion a negative sign. In Clausius' convention W is the work done BY the gas, which is positive when the gas expands.
At constant pressure W = PΔV. ΔV = 5.0 − 2.0 = 3.0 dm³ = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³, so W = 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa × 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ = 450 J. It is positive because the gas expands and does work on its surroundings.

A student who multiplies the pressure by the final volume, 1.5 × 10⁵ × 5.0 × 10⁻³ = 750 J, has calculated PV, not the work. Work depends on the change in volume: W = PΔV = 1.5 × 10⁵ × 3.0 × 10⁻³ = 450 J.
A student who substitutes ΔV = 3.0 without converting dm³ to m³ gets an answer 1000 times too large. 1 dm³ = 10⁻³ m³, so ΔV = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ and W = 450 J.
questions.explain: At constant pressure W = PΔV. ΔV = 5.0 − 2.0 = 3.0 dm³ = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³, so W = 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa × 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ = 450 J. It is positive because the gas expands and does work on its surroundings.
questions.working: Constant pressure, so W = PΔV. ΔV = 5.0 dm³ − 2.0 dm³ = 3.0 dm³ = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³. W = 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa × 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ = 4.5 × 10² J. The gas expands, so the work done by it is positive: W = +4.5 × 10² J.

questions.q: A sample of 8.0 g of helium, a monatomic ideal gas of molar mass 4.0 g mol⁻¹, is heated at constant pressure from 20 °C to 80 °C. The thermal energy supplied is 2.49 × 10³ J. R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the change in internal energy ΔU of the helium?
optionWhy: A student who thinks all the thermal energy supplied becomes internal energy picks the value of Q. At constant pressure the gas expands and does work, W = nRΔT = 997 J, so ΔU = Q − W = 1.5 × 10³ J.
n = 8.0 g ÷ 4.0 g mol⁻¹ = 2.0 mol and ΔT = 60 K. ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT = 1.5 × 2.0 × 8.31 × 60 = 1.5 × 10³ J. The rest of the 2.5 × 10³ J supplied leaves as work done by the expanding gas.
A student who adds 273 to the temperature change uses ΔT = 333 K. A change of 60 °C is a change of 60 K, so ΔU = 1.5 × 2.0 × 8.31 × 60 = 1.5 × 10³ J.
A student who uses the mass, 8.0, as the amount of substance gets a value four times too large. n = m/M = 8.0 g ÷ 4.0 g mol⁻¹ = 2.0 mol.
questions.explain: n = 8.0 g ÷ 4.0 g mol⁻¹ = 2.0 mol and ΔT = 60 K. ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT = 1.5 × 2.0 × 8.31 × 60 = 1.5 × 10³ J. The rest of the 2.5 × 10³ J supplied leaves as work done by the expanding gas.
questions.working: n = m/M = 8.0 g ÷ 4.0 g mol⁻¹ = 2.0 mol. ΔT = 80 °C − 20 °C = 60 K. ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT = 1.5 × 2.0 mol × 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 60 K = 1496 J ≈ 1.5 × 10³ J. (Check: W = PΔV = nRΔT = 997 J, and ΔU + W = 2.5 × 10³ J = Q.)

questions.q: Which statement correctly relates the entropy of a system to its particles?
options: Entropy is the total kinetic energy of all the particles, so it is measured in joules.
Entropy is how untidy the objects in a system look, whatever their particles are doing.
The more ways the particles can be arranged, the greater their disorder and entropy.
Entropy, like energy, is conserved, so the particles keep the same disorder.
optionWhy: A student who thinks entropy is a form of energy picks this. Entropy is measured in J K⁻¹, not J, and it can change with no change in energy, as in the free expansion of a gas.
A student who takes 'disorder' in its everyday sense picks this. Thermodynamic entropy concerns the arrangements of particles; rearranging large objects changes it negligibly.

Entropy relates to the degree of disorder of the particles: the more arrangements of positions and energies are consistent with the macrostate, the greater the entropy. This is why a gas has more entropy than the same substance as a liquid or solid.

A student who assumes every thermodynamic quantity is conserved picks this. Entropy is not conserved: it increases in every irreversible process in an isolated system, and the disorder of the particles changes when, for example, a solid melts.
questions.explain: Entropy relates to the degree of disorder of the particles: the more arrangements of positions and energies are consistent with the macrostate, the greater the entropy. This is why a gas has more entropy than the same substance as a liquid or solid.

questions.q: Helium, a monatomic ideal gas, expands reversibly and isothermally at 27 °C, doing 600 J of work on its surroundings. What is the entropy change of the helium?
options: +2.0 J K⁻¹, as Q = W = 600 J is supplied to it at 300 K
0 J K⁻¹, as no heat is transferred at a constant temperature
−2.0 J K⁻¹, as the gas does work, so W = −600 J and Q = −600 J
+22 J K⁻¹, as Q = 600 J is supplied at a temperature of 27 °C
optionWhy: At constant temperature ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas, so Q = ΔU + W = 600 J of thermal energy is supplied to the helium at T = 300 K. ΔS = ΔQ/T = 600 ÷ 300 = +2.0 J K⁻¹.

A student who thinks constant temperature means no heat transfer sets ΔQ = 0. The expanding gas does 600 J of work while its internal energy stays constant, so 600 J of thermal energy must be supplied, and its entropy rises.
A student who treats the work done by the gas as negative gets Q = ΔU + W = −600 J. In Clausius' convention work done BY the gas is positive, W = +600 J, so Q = +600 J and the entropy increases.
A student who divides by 27, the temperature in °C, gets 22 J K⁻¹. ΔS = ΔQ/T needs the absolute temperature, 27 + 273 = 300 K.
questions.explain: At constant temperature ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas, so Q = ΔU + W = 600 J of thermal energy is supplied to the helium at T = 300 K. ΔS = ΔQ/T = 600 ÷ 300 = +2.0 J K⁻¹.
questions.working: Isothermal, ideal gas: ΔU = 0, so Q = ΔU + W = 0 + 600 J = 600 J (supplied to the gas). T = 27 + 273 = 300 K, constant and the process reversible, so ΔS = ΔQ/T = 600 J ÷ 300 K = +2.0 J K⁻¹.

questions.q: Which of the following is a correct statement of the second law of thermodynamics in its Clausius form?
options: Thermal energy cannot be moved from a colder body to a hotter body by any means at all.
Thermal energy cannot flow spontaneously from a colder body to a hotter body.
Thermal energy flows spontaneously from the body with more internal energy to the one with less.
Cold flows spontaneously from a colder body into a hotter body until their temperatures are equal.
optionWhy: A student who drops the word 'spontaneously' picks this. A refrigerator moves thermal energy from its cold interior to the warmer room; this is allowed because work is done on it.

This is the Clausius form. The word 'spontaneously' matters: thermal energy can be moved from cold to hot, as in a refrigerator, but only when work is done, so the transfer is not the sole result of the process.

A student who confuses internal energy with temperature picks this. The direction of heat flow is set by temperature: a warm bath with a large internal energy still receives heat from a small, hotter cup of tea.
A student who thinks of cold as something that moves picks this. There is no substance called cold; cooling means thermal energy flowing out of the hotter body into the colder one.
questions.explain: This is the Clausius form. The word 'spontaneously' matters: thermal energy can be moved from cold to hot, as in a refrigerator, but only when work is done, so the transfer is not the sole result of the process.

questions.q: Which statement of the second law of thermodynamics in terms of entropy is correct for an isolated system?
options: Its entropy increases in every process, whether the process is reversible or not.
Its entropy is constant in every process, as entropy is conserved like energy.
Its entropy increases only when its temperature rises and is otherwise fixed.
Its entropy stays constant in reversible processes and increases in irreversible processes.
optionWhy: A student who has learned the slogan 'entropy always increases' picks this. In a reversible process the entropy of an isolated system stays constant; it increases only in irreversible processes.
A student who assumes entropy is conserved like energy picks this. Entropy is created in irreversible processes, so the entropy of an isolated system increases in any real process.
A student who thinks entropy is measured by temperature or thermal energy picks this. Entropy can increase at constant temperature, as when ice melts or a gas expands freely.
This is the entropy form of the second law: the entropy of an isolated system never decreases. It is unchanged in an idealized reversible process and increases in an irreversible one.
questions.explain: This is the entropy form of the second law: the entropy of an isolated system never decreases. It is unchanged in an idealized reversible process and increases in an irreversible one.

questions.q: A hot copper block and a cold copper block are placed in contact inside a sealed, perfectly insulated box, so that together they form an isolated system. They reach a common temperature. Which statement about entropy is correct?
options: The total entropy is unchanged, because the entropy lost by the hot block is gained by the cold block.
The total entropy increases, because heat flow across a temperature difference is irreversible.
The entropy of each block increases, because thermal energy flows between the two blocks.
The total entropy increases, because some of the energy is destroyed as the blocks come to equilibrium.
optionWhy: A student who thinks entropy is conserved picks this. The cold block gains Q/T_c, which is larger than the Q/T_h lost by the hot block, so the total increases.
Heat flow from a hotter to a colder body is irreversible, so the entropy of the isolated system increases. The hot block loses entropy Q/T_h, and the cold block gains more, Q/T_c, because T_c < T_h.
A student who thinks the entropy of every object must increase picks this. The hot block loses thermal energy and its entropy decreases; only the total entropy must increase.

A student who thinks irreversible processes destroy energy picks this. The total energy of the isolated system is unchanged; the entropy increases because the process is irreversible, not because energy is lost.
questions.explain: Heat flow from a hotter to a colder body is irreversible, so the entropy of the isolated system increases. The hot block loses entropy Q/T_h, and the cold block gains more, Q/T_c, because T_c < T_h.

questions.q: Water placed in the freezer compartment of a refrigerator freezes, and the entropy of the water decreases. The refrigerator stands in a kitchen. Which statement explains why this is consistent with the second law of thermodynamics?
options: The refrigerator transfers thermal energy to the kitchen, whose entropy rises by at least as much as the water's falls.
The entropy lost by the water is passed to the air inside the freezer, so the total entropy is unchanged.
The water is not isolated; no thermal energy can pass to the warmer kitchen, whose entropy is unchanged.
The work done by the refrigerator allows the total entropy to decrease, so no increase elsewhere is needed.
optionWhy: The water is not an isolated system, so its entropy can decrease locally. The refrigerator delivers to the kitchen the thermal energy removed from the water plus the work done on it, and the entropy of the kitchen increases by an equal or greater amount.

A student who thinks entropy is conserved picks this. The freezer air is also being cooled, and its entropy falls too. The compensating increase is in the kitchen, and for a real, irreversible refrigerator it exceeds the decrease.

A student who thinks thermal energy can never pass from a colder body to a hotter one, by any means, rules out any effect on the kitchen. A refrigerator uses work to transfer thermal energy from its cold interior to the warmer kitchen, and the kitchen's entropy rises by at least as much as the water's falls.

A student who thinks doing work can override the second law picks this. Work lets the water's entropy fall, but the total entropy of water plus surroundings cannot decrease: the kitchen's entropy rises to compensate.
questions.explain: The water is not an isolated system, so its entropy can decrease locally. The refrigerator delivers to the kitchen the thermal energy removed from the water plus the work done on it, and the entropy of the kitchen increases by an equal or greater amount.

questions.q: Which statement about a thermodynamic process of a fixed mass of monatomic ideal gas is correct?
options: Adiabatic: the temperature is kept fixed, so ΔU = 0 and Q = W.
Adiabatic: no thermal energy is transferred, so Q = 0 and W = −ΔU.
Isothermal: the temperature is kept fixed, so no thermal energy flows.
Isobaric: all of the thermal energy supplied becomes internal energy.
optionWhy: A student who confuses adiabatic with isothermal picks this. Adiabatic means no heat transfer (Q = 0); the temperature changes because work changes the internal energy.
An adiabatic process is defined by Q = 0. The first law then gives 0 = ΔU + W, so W = −ΔU: work done by the gas lowers its internal energy, and work done on it raises it.
A student who thinks constant temperature means no heat transfer picks this. At constant temperature ΔU = 0, so Q = W: an expanding gas must be supplied with exactly as much heat as the work it does.
A student who thinks heat supplied all becomes internal energy picks this. At constant pressure the gas expands and does work PΔV, so Q = ΔU + PΔV = (5/2)nRΔT, of which only (3/2)nRΔT is ΔU.
questions.explain: An adiabatic process is defined by Q = 0. The first law then gives 0 = ΔU + W, so W = −ΔU: work done by the gas lowers its internal energy, and work done on it raises it.
questions.working: Adiabatic: Q = 0 by definition, so Q = ΔU + W gives 0 = ΔU + W, i.e. W = −ΔU. Isothermal: ΔU = 0, so Q = W (not zero when the volume changes). Isobaric: Q = ΔU + PΔV, so Q ≠ ΔU when the gas expands.

questions.q: Helium, a monatomic ideal gas, has a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and a volume of 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³. It is compressed adiabatically to a volume of 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³. For this process PV^(5/3) = constant. What is the final pressure of the helium?
optionWhy: A student who uses PV = constant treats the compression as isothermal. In an adiabatic compression the temperature rises, so the pressure rises by 3.0^(5/3) = 6.24, not 3.
A student who uses the exponent 3/5 instead of 5/3 gets 3.0^(3/5) = 1.93. Solving PV^(5/3) = constant for P gives P₂ = P₁(V₁/V₂)^(5/3).
P₂ = P₁(V₁/V₂)^(5/3) = 1.0 × 10⁵ × 3.0^(5/3) = 1.0 × 10⁵ × 6.24 = 6.2 × 10⁵ Pa. The pressure rises by more than the factor of 3 an isothermal compression would give, because the gas also warms.
A student who writes the volume ratio as V₂/V₁ gets (1/3)^(5/3) = 0.160, a pressure that falls on compression. From P₁V₁^(5/3) = P₂V₂^(5/3), P₂ = P₁(V₁/V₂)^(5/3).
questions.explain: P₂ = P₁(V₁/V₂)^(5/3) = 1.0 × 10⁵ × 3.0^(5/3) = 1.0 × 10⁵ × 6.24 = 6.2 × 10⁵ Pa. The pressure rises by more than the factor of 3 an isothermal compression would give, because the gas also warms.

questions.q: The working gas of a heat engine is taken round one complete cycle, returning to its initial state. Which statement about the cycle is correct?
options: The net work done by the gas is zero, as the gas returns to the state it started in.
The net work done by the gas is the work it does while it expands, as compression is not output.
ΔU = 0, so the net thermal energy supplied to the gas equals the net work done by the gas.
ΔU is positive, because thermal energy is supplied to the gas in every cycle of the engine.
optionWhy: A student who treats work as a property of the state picks this. The net work done in a cycle is the area enclosed on the P–V diagram; for an engine it is positive, which is the whole purpose of the engine.

A student who counts only the expansion stroke picks this. The gas must be compressed again, and work is done on it then; the net work done by the gas is the expansion work minus the compression work, the area enclosed on the P–V diagram.
Internal energy is a property of the state, and the gas returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0 for the cycle. Q = ΔU + W then gives Q = W: the net heat supplied equals the net work done.
A student who thinks supplied heat builds up in the gas picks this. Over a complete cycle the gas returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0; the heat supplied leaves as work and as heat rejected.
questions.explain: Internal energy is a property of the state, and the gas returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0 for the cycle. Q = ΔU + W then gives Q = W: the net heat supplied equals the net work done.
questions.working: U is a property of the state and the gas returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0 over the cycle. Q = ΔU + W then gives net Q = net W; for an engine both are positive and equal to the area enclosed by the cycle on the P–V diagram.

questions.q: A heat engine works between reservoirs at 600 K and 300 K. In each cycle it absorbs 2.5 kJ of thermal energy from the hot reservoir and rejects 1.8 kJ of thermal energy to the cold reservoir. What is the efficiency of the engine?
optionWhy: A student who divides the energy rejected by the energy supplied, 1.8 ÷ 2.5, has calculated the fraction wasted. Efficiency is the useful work divided by the input: 0.7 ÷ 2.5 = 28%.
A student who divides the work by the energy rejected, 0.7 ÷ 1.8, has used the wrong denominator. The input energy is the 2.5 kJ absorbed from the hot reservoir.
A student who uses 1 − T_c/T_h = 1 − 300/600 has found the Carnot efficiency, the maximum for these reservoirs. This engine's actual efficiency is W/Q_h = 28%.
Useful work per cycle W = Q_h − Q_c = 2.5 − 1.8 = 0.7 kJ. η = W/Q_h = 0.7 ÷ 2.5 = 0.28 = 28%. This is below the Carnot limit of 50% for these reservoirs, as it must be.
questions.explain: Useful work per cycle W = Q_h − Q_c = 2.5 − 1.8 = 0.7 kJ. η = W/Q_h = 0.7 ÷ 2.5 = 0.28 = 28%. This is below the Carnot limit of 50% for these reservoirs, as it must be.
questions.working: W = Q_h − Q_c = 2.5 kJ − 1.8 kJ = 0.7 kJ. η = W/Q_h = 0.7 kJ ÷ 2.5 kJ = 0.28 = 28%. (Carnot limit 1 − 300/600 = 50%, so the engine is possible.)

questions.q: A Carnot engine works between a hot reservoir at 227 °C and a cold reservoir at 27 °C. In each cycle it absorbs 1200 J of thermal energy from the hot reservoir. How much work does it do in each cycle?
optionWhy: A student who substitutes the Celsius temperatures gets η = 1 − 27/227 = 0.88 and W = 1060 J. η_Carnot = 1 − T_c/T_h needs kelvin: 1 − 300/500 = 0.40.
A student who takes T_c/T_h = 0.60 as the efficiency has calculated the fraction of the input rejected to the cold reservoir. The efficiency is 1 − 0.60 = 0.40, so W = 480 J.
A student who divides the temperature difference by the cold temperature, 200/300, has used the wrong denominator. η_Carnot = (T_h − T_c)/T_h = 200/500 = 0.40.

questions.q: Which statement about the Carnot cycle and its efficiency is correct?
options: A Carnot engine is 100% efficient, since its cycle is reversible and has no friction.
The Carnot efficiency is unchanged if both temperatures are raised by the same number of kelvin.
No engine working between two given reservoirs can be more efficient than a Carnot engine.
The Carnot efficiency is T_c/T_h, the ratio of the cold to the hot reservoir temperature.
optionWhy: A student who thinks friction is the only cause of inefficiency picks this. A Carnot engine must still reject thermal energy to the cold reservoir; its efficiency is 1 − T_c/T_h, which is less than 1.
A student who thinks the efficiency depends only on the temperature difference picks this. η = (T_h − T_c)/T_h: with the same difference but a larger T_h, the efficiency falls.
The Carnot cycle is reversible, and the second law shows that no engine working between the same two reservoirs can exceed its efficiency, 1 − T_c/T_h.
A student who confuses efficiency with the fraction of energy rejected picks this. T_c/T_h is the fraction rejected to the cold reservoir; the efficiency is 1 − T_c/T_h.
questions.explain: The Carnot cycle is reversible, and the second law shows that no engine working between the same two reservoirs can exceed its efficiency, 1 − T_c/T_h.
